anchor: The same clause also closes the circle of divine judgment and royal restoration announced earlier in the chapter.  Nathan’s oracle (vv 10-12) declared that because David “despised” the LORD by taking Uriah’s wife, the sword would never depart from his house; yet once David confessed, “I have sinned against the LORD,” the prophet answered, “Now the LORD has put away your sin” (vv 13-14).  The death of the first child born to Bathsheba fulfilled the threatened penalty, and David’s subsequent worship and renewed marital union with her (vv 20-24) mark a re-ordered relationship with the LORD.  By stepping forward to capture Rabbah, David re-assumes the military leadership that had slackened while he remained in Jerusalem, and the victory—together with the birth of Solomon, “loved” by the LORD (v 24-25)—demonstrates that the divine favor pronounced through Nathan is already taking effect.  Thus the taking of Rabbah functions as both a practical and a symbolic affirmation that, after judgment, the king is once again acting in concert with the LORD’s purposes for Israel.

anchor: The related scriptures echo the same sequence.  1 Timothy 6:9 says those who seek riches “fall into temptation and are trapped by many senseless and harmful desires,” a line that mirrors Alma’s grief over hearts swallowed by costly apparel and pride.  1 Nephi 12:17 and 15:24 call temptations “mists of darkness” and “fiery darts” that blind and lead away; the Zoramites, by ceasing daily supplication, walk into that mist and are blinded to their own prideful prayer.  1 Corinthians 10:13 promises that when testing comes God “will also provide the way out so that you may be able to endure it,” yet the Zoramites never take the way out because they never ask.  2 Corinthians 11:3 warns of thoughts “led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ,” exactly what Alma sees as their prayer boasts of being “chosen” while denying Christ.  Together these passages reinforce the verse’s warning: neglect of daily prayer is not a neutral omission but the moment temptation is given room to settle, harden, and finally dictate worship.

anchor: Esther 9:30 states that “letters were sent wishing peace and security to all the Jews, to the one hundred twenty-seven provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus.”  Within the chapter this sentence forms the final, stabilizing act after the violence has ended.  First the Jews had defended themselves and killed their enemies (vv 5-16); then they rested, feasted, and instituted Purim (vv 17-19).  Mordecai next recorded these events and sent an initial letter requiring annual observance (vv 20-23).  Esther’s own letter, jointly authorized with Mordecai (v 29), repeats the command but adds the explicit wish for “peace and security.”  Thus the verse shifts the narrative from wartime deliverance to settled, ongoing communal life: the same imperial post that once carried Haman’s decree of destruction (3:12-15) now carries words that protect and unite the scattered Jewish population.
